title: Deep learning identifies antimicrobial peptides hidden in prion-related proteins
summary: APEX 1.1 screened 19.3 million peptide fragments from 2,897 prion-related proteins and identified 1,179 candidate antimicrobial peptides, termed prionins. Among 75 synthesized candidates, 59 inhibited at least one tested bacterial strain; two selected peptides reduced Acinetobacter baumannii burden in a mouse skin-abscess model. The study shows that prion-related sequences can yield experimentally active antimicrobial fragments, but does not show that these peptides are naturally released or function as host-defense agents in their source organisms.
ai_technology: APEX 1.1 deep-learning antimicrobial-peptide prediction and prioritization

evidence.tested: Of 75 synthesized APEX-selected prionins, 59 inhibited at least one bacterial strain in vitro; two selected peptides reduced A. baumannii burden in a mouse skin-abscess model.
evidence.unknown: No evidence shows these fragments are naturally released from their source proteins or physiologically function as host-defense peptides in native organisms. Mouse results do not establish human efficacy or safety.
evidence.ai_role: APEX 1.1 scored peptide fragments for predicted antimicrobial activity and prioritized candidates from a search across prion-related proteins for synthesis and experimental screening.
